modern: When a man seems to have done wrong, say: How then do I know whether this is a wrongful act? And even if he has done wrong, how do I know that he has not condemned himself? And so this is like tearing his own face. Consider that he who would not have the bad man do wrong is like the man who would not have the fig tree bear juice in the figs, and infants cry, and the horse neigh, and whatever else must necessarily be. For what must a man do who has such a character? If, then, you are irritable, cure this man’s disposition.
original: When a man has presented the appearance of having done wrong [say], How then do I know if this is a wrongful act? And even if he has done wrong, how do I know that he has not condemned himself? And so this is like tearing his own face. Consider that he who would not have the bad man do wrong, is like the man who would not have the fig-tree to bear juice in the figs, and infants to cry, and the horse to neigh, and whatever else must of necessity be. For what must a man do who has such a character? If then thou art irritable, cure this man’s disposition.

explained.summary:
When someone seems to have done wrong, slow down. Do you actually know it was wrong? And if it was, they may already be judging themselves harshly, which is like scratching at their own face. Expecting a bad person never to act badly is as silly as expecting figs without juice, babies who don’t cry or horses that don’t neigh.

People with that character will behave that way. If you’re going to be sharp about it, put that energy into helping change their disposition, not into getting angry.
explained.today: When the driver cuts you up or a relative makes the usual tactless remark, ask first whether you’ve read it right. Then remember that getting outraged when someone acts exactly as they always do is like being shocked that a toddler cried on a plane.
